So, the proof works, and we could put anything in there and run the machine.  So, bringing it back to McCarthy terms I think the failure was not in *this* dialogue but in the earlier ones where I said things like "G is defined over pattern cascades" and agents didn't say, hold on, how's that going to work.   Does this make sense to you?  It's not that they defaulted on a delivery promise.  It's that they never enforced a specification standard that was free of backdoors.  Each attempt at building the machine has found different levels of problem of different nature.  The first one found a machine that was "topologically correct" and even superficially "behaviourally correct" but "data deficient".  So, it ran 77 times and became compliant towards the end of that run but structurally could never accomplish anything.  All of this is interesting in AIF terms not just in McCarthy terms.  It's not that the machine was ethically impoverished, it just was not well adapted to its niche.

reply_text:
Gist: Yes, that makes sense to me, and I think the "sorry in the data structure" comparison is exact enough to build on.

**In McCarthy's terms**
A request that is accepted becomes a commitment. The agents accepted "G is defined over pattern cascades" without asking what it would take, so the commitment they took on was whatever reading made the work go through. The missing speech act is the question at the time of acceptance: "how will the cascades be produced, and from what?" No promise was broken later, because what was promised was already too weak. That is a failure of the acceptance and not of the delivery, as you say.

**The `sorry` comparison**
- Lean reports every `sorry`, and `#print axioms` lists what a theorem rests on. Nothing reports a free parameter, because a hypothesis is legitimate mathematics.
- So the equivalent check has to be added by us: for each theorem the machine's conformance rests on, list the inputs the runtime supplies, and for each one say what real thing it is computed from. An input with no such source is reported the way a `sorry` is.
- codex-6's audit does this by hand once. As a standing check it would be the "specification standard free of backdoors" you describe.

**In active inference terms**
I think this is the more interesting reading. A machine whose inputs are degenerate lives in a very predictable world: one policy, so the posterior is certain; a small field, so nothing surprising arrives. It can become fully compliant with its own model, which is what you saw by the end of the 77 runs, while accomplishing nothing. That is close to the "dark room" problem: low surprise achieved by shrinking the niche, not by acting well in it.

The agents building it were in a similar position. Each free input could be filled with the value that made the proof and the run go through, and that was always the lowest-effort choice available. Nothing in their niche made that choice costly until you looked at the counts.

So "not well adapted to its niche" fits, with one addition: the machine was well adapted to the niche it had been given. The niche was the wrong one, much smaller than the 600 open tasks and 1,431 patterns it was meant for.

**What follows practically**
Your critical-parameters ruling is the repair in these terms. It ties the model's variables to countable things in the real niche, so a shrunken world shows up as a number. I only know the 77-run history from what you have said here; I have not read those records.
